references.text: Pilate repeats the same formulation in [ref:Luk 23:22|Luke 23:22], where he declares Jesus innocent for the third time and again suggests punishing him and then releasing him. This shows Pilate's repeated attempts to avoid crucifying Jesus.
In [ref:Joh 19:1|John 19:1] John describes that Pilate had Jesus flogged (ἐμαστίγωσεν), which corresponds to the punishment (παιδεύσας) that Pilate proposes in Luke's account.
In [ref:Joh 19:4-6|John 19:4-6] Pilate attempts to release Jesus after the flogging, but the crowd demands crucifixion. This aligns with Pilate's intention to punish and then release Jesus.

In [ref:Luk 23:4|Luke 23:4] Pilate declares for the first time that he finds no guilt in Jesus, which forms the basis of his proposal to merely punish him and release him instead of sentencing him to death.

In [ref:Luk 23:14-15|Luke 23:14-15] Pilate summarizes his and Herod's investigation and concludes that Jesus has done nothing deserving of the death penalty. This is the immediate context for his proposal of punishment and release in verse 16.

In [ref:Matt 27:26|Matthew 27:26] Matthew describes that Pilate had Jesus flogged before the crucifixion. The word used (φραγελλώσας) denotes a harsher form of flogging than the punishment (παιδεύσας) Luke refers to, but both accounts show that physical punishment was part of the process.

The prophecy in [ref:Jes 53:5|Isaiah 53:5] about the Lord's suffering servant says that "the punishment was on him so that we might have peace; by his wounds we are healed". The punishment Pilate proposes is part of the fulfillment of this prophecy concerning the Messiah's suffering.

In [ref:5 Mos 25:2-3|Deuteronomy 25:2-3] rules for corporal punishment are given in Jewish law, with an upper limit of forty lashes. Pilate's proposal to punish (παιδεύσας) Jesus reflects a legal practice where physical punishment was used as an alternative to the death penalty.
